fact_en:
Why are dragonflies so common around rice fields?

Because they love to eat mosquitoes and other small insects that live near the water in the rice fields!
fact_bis:
Nganong sagad ang mga tambayayong sa palibot sa humayan?

Tungod kay mokaon sila og mga lamok ug uban pang gagmay nga insekto nga nagpuyo duol sa tubig sa humayan!

findings.note: Card is 'Rice Field Insects' / 'Why are dragonflies so common around rice fields?'. The Cebuano names them 'tambayayong', which is not an animal at all — everywhere else in this corpus tambayayong is the verb for cooperating/working together (ffct-02113 'nakigtambayayong kini sa ubo', ffct-28377 'Nagtambayayong ang mga mag-uuma ug karabaw', dcard-07261 collaboration). Dragonfly in this corpus is consistently alindahaw / alindanaw / tutubi across ~35 cards. The card body never names the insect any other way, so a child reading only the Cebuano is told that 'cooperations' are common around rice fields and eat mosquitoes — the animal the fact is about is unrecoverable from the card.

fact_en:
How do caterpillars and human children grow differently?

A caterpillar sheds its skin several times to grow, but a human child grows without shedding skin!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang kalainan sa pagtubo sa hantatalo ug bata nga tawo?

Ang hantatalo mag-ilis sa panit sa makadaghang higayon aron motubo, apan ang bata motubo nga dili mag-ilis sa panit!

findings.note: title_bis "Hodhod vs Tawo" for "Caterpillar vs Human". Hodhod/hudhod is to grate or scrape, not an insect — it names no caterpillar in any dialect, and it is the ONLY occurrence in the whole 320-batch sweep, against ulod 169x, hantatalo 5x, higad 3x. The card's own body uses the correct word ("Ang hantatalo mag-ilis sa panit..."), so the title is the clear outlier. A child reading the heading alone is told the comparison is between a scraping action and a human.

fact_en: A tadpole swims in water, but a chick walks on land, showing how frog and chicken young move in very different ways!
fact_bis: Ang boto molangoy sa tubig, apan ang piso maglakaw sa yuta, mao nga lahi kaayo ang lihok sa anak sa baki ug manok!

findings.note: Body: "Ang boto molangoy sa tubig, apan ang piso maglakaw sa yuta..." — boto means VOTE (confirmed elsewhere in this same corpus: ffct-37629 "Boto sa Konsensus"), or buto = seed/to explode. The subject of the card's main sentence is therefore a different thing than the tadpole. Lower severity than the first: title_bis is correctly "Butete vs Sisiw" and the clause ends "...ang anak sa baki ug manok", so an attentive child can recover the fact; flagged because the swap is to a real, unrelated word rather than a near-miss spelling, and butete is used 72x elsewhere in the sweep.

fact_en:
How do marble and schist form in the Philippines?

They are metamorphic rocks! Ancient plate collisions squeezed and heated them, leaving behind cool geological evidence.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagporma sa marmol ug schist sa Pilipinas?

Sila mga metamorphic rocks! Gipislit ug gipainit sila sa mga karaang pagbangga sa plato, nga nagbilin sa ebidensiyang geological.

findings.note: Body: "Gipislit ug gipainit sila sa mga karaang pagbangga sa plato" for "Ancient plate collisions squeezed and heated them". In Cebuano *plato* is a dinner plate; a tectonic plate is *plaka* (or the English "plate"). Nothing else in this card names crust, tectonics or the plate concept, so a Cebuano-only reader is told marble and schist were formed by ancient collisions of dishes. The card's own terms list carries the same defect in Tagalog ("banggaan ng plato"), i.e. it is a translation-pipeline error, not regional usage.

fact_en:
Where do gold and copper hide in the Philippines?

Near volcanic arcs! These gold and copper mines formed from hot fluids at plate boundaries.
fact_bis:
Asa nagtago ang bulawan ug tumbaga sa Pilipinas?

Duol sa mga volcanic arc! Ang mga minahan sa bulawan ug tumbaga naporma gikan sa init nga mga pluwido sa mga utlanan sa plato.

findings.note: Body: "init nga mga pluwido sa mga utlanan sa plato" for "hot fluids at plate boundaries". *Utlanan sa plato* reads as the rim of a dinner plate; the correct term is *utlanan sa plaka* (plate boundary). The mention of volcanic arcs gives geological setting but never restores the plate concept, so the card's central claim about where gold and copper form is lost. (Contrast ffct-37576, which also titles it "Paglihok sa Plato" but is a PASS because its body says "Philippine Sea Plate" in English and restores the meaning.)

fact_en:
What are the Philippine islands made of?

Many terranes — crustal fragments that were welded together by plate collisions over millions of years!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang mga isla sa Pilipinas?

Daghang mga terrane — mga piraso sa crust nga gipahiusa sa mga pagbangga sa plato sa minilyon ka mga tuig!

findings.note: Body: "mga piraso sa crust nga gipahiusa sa mga pagbangga sa plato" for "crustal fragments welded together by plate collisions". *Plato* = dinner plate; the card's OWN terms field lists the correct word *plaka*, so the intended noun exists in the record but never reaches the Cebuano text. The fact being taught (the islands are terranes joined by tectonic-plate collisions) is not recoverable from the Cebuano alone.

fact_en:
What should you do before using the key?

Sort the rock samples into rough piles by one big feature, like having layers or not!
fact_bis:
Unsay buhaton sa dili pa gamiton ang key?

Bahina ang rock samples ngadto sa baga nga mga tapok pinaagi sa usa ka dako nga feature, sama sa adunay layers o wala!

findings.note: title_bis "Pag-ay sa Bato" (title_en "Sorting Rocks"). "Pag-ay" is not a Cebuano word — it is the only occurrence of that token in the entire 337-batch corpus, so it is a one-off, not a dialect form. It is either a broken "paghan-ay" (to arrange/sort, the correct word) or a broken "pag-ayo" (to repair — the corpus uses "Pag-ayo sa mga Guba nga Butang" for Repairing), and the second reading names a different activity than sorting. Lower confidence than the first flag: the body ("Bahina ang rock samples ngadto sa ... mga tapok pinaagi sa usa ka dako nga feature") does deliver the sorting instruction, so the fact itself is recoverable; flagged because the shipped title word is objectively not a word rather than merely clumsy.

fact_en:
How do your kidneys and lungs team up?

They keep your blood's pH stable! Kidneys remove acids while lungs balance carbon dioxide levels — a perfect duo for healthy blood.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagtinabangay sa kidneys ug lungs?

Gipapabilin nila ang stable nga pH sa imong dugo! Nagkuha ang kidneys ug acids samtang gibalanse sa lungs ang carbon dioxide levels — perfect duo para sa healthy nga dugo.

findings.note: title_bis "Kidney ug Bag pH" (title_en "Kidney & Lung pH"). Cebuano for lungs is BAGA; "Bag" is not that word. Corpus triage: I scanned all 337 batches for a standalone token "Bag" — 78 of 79 hits are the English noun bag (Go-Bag, plastic bag, backpack), so a reader parses this title as "Kidney and Bag pH", naming a container instead of an organ. The card's own body uses the correct term ("gibalanse sa lungs ang carbon dioxide levels"), the classic title-outlier signature. Title is short (16 chars) so this is not title-length truncation.

fact_en: Use the exact same pot with the same drainage holes so water drains equally in all your setups!
fact_bis: Gamita ang eksaktong parehas nga paso ug lungag sa paagusan aron parehas ang pagtulo sa tubig sa tanang setup!

findings.note: title_bis "Parehas nga Kolon" for "Same Pot Drainage": kolon is the earthen COOKING pot (palayok), not a plant pot with drainage holes. The card's own body uses the right word ("eksaktong parehas nga paso ug lungag sa paagusan"), so the title names a different object than the experiment it heads.

fact_en:
Is every inherited color-vision change bad?

Not always! Some are harmful for certain tasks but nearly neutral for others. That's why we must name the job when labeling an effect!
fact_bis:
Makadaot ba ang tanan nga inherited color-vision change?

Dili kanunay! Ang uban harmful para sa pipila ka buluhaton pero halos neutral sa uban. Mao nga dapat nganlan ang trabaho kon mag-label sa epekto!

findings.note: title_bis "Pagkabulag sa Kolor" for "Color Blindness": Cebuano bulag = TO SEPARATE/part ways (blind is buta), so the title reads "separation of colour". Nothing in the body names the condition in Cebuano — it only says "inherited color-vision change" in English — so the title is never corrected.

fact_en: Tension arrows point along the rope or string, pulling away from the object where they attach!
fact_bis: Ang mga arrow sa tension nagtudlo subay sa pisi o hilo, nagbira palayo sa butang diin kini gitaod!

findings.note: bis "nagtudlo subay sa pisi o hilo" for "along the rope or string": Cebuano hilo = POISON (thread is tanod), so the sentence reads "along the rope or poison". Confirmed false-friend class; only the adjacent "pisi" keeps the sentence usable.

fact_en:
Why rotate the pots every two days?

Give each pot a quarter turn! This helps every plant get equal light from all sides.
fact_bis:
Ngano nga tuyoka ang mga paso matag duha ka adlaw?

Tuyoka ang matag paso og quarter turn! Makakuha ang matag tanom og patas nga kahayag gikan sa tanang kilid.

findings.note: title_bis "Pagtuyok sa Kolon" for "Pot Rotation": same swap — kolon = cooking pot, while the body correctly says "tuyoka ang matag paso". Title tells the child to rotate a cooking pot.
